14: Reactive, not planned. Black's g8-knight is still undeveloped (moved there on move 4 and never left) -- that's the real problem on the board. Instead, Hongnam reacted to the bishop sitting on f4 and played g5 to attack it. The bishop just retreats to g3 for free, and g5 leaves two permanent kingside holes (g7/h6) with nothing to show for it. Eval: +156 -> +367. Engine wanted d5, hitting the center and freeing the g8-knight instead.
26: Right diagnosis, wrong square. Hongnam correctly identified the danger (White's rooks connected after O-O-O) and tried to get the king to safety -- but Kd7 puts the king directly on the d-file, the exact file White's rook just landed on, right as the e5-pawn is about to crack it open. Eval: +542 -> +749. Engine wanted Ne7, simple development instead of a king move at all.
37: White's own mistake, not Hongnam's -- Qg4+ was weaker than the engine's quiet d6-push. Worth remembering for Hongnam's own games: a forcing check isn't automatically the best move just because it's forcing. Ke8 in reply was fine, no issue.
43: Another White mistake: Qe6+ forces a trade sequence (Be5/Qe7/Qxe7+/Bxc7) that nets a pawn but trades queens, handing back some of the advantage by simplifying (+619 -> +256 by move 24) instead of the quiet Qb4, which wins both queenside pawns with no trade at all. Same lesson as move 37, mirrored: when you're already ahead, the forcing move isn't always the best one.
52: Hongnam's most interesting move of the game -- this one had a real plan for once, not pure reflex: f5 genuinely denies White's knight the e4 square (a real minor threat, worth a pawn) and frees f6 for the long-stuck g8-knight. But it triages wrong: it answers a small threat while ignoring a bigger one one square further down the same diagonal idea -- Nd5 followed by Nb6+, forking king and rook for a full rook. Engine wanted b5, which denies Nb6 directly. Eval: +372 -> +712. The refined pattern: not 'reflexive', but 'doesn't rank multiple threats by how much they actually cost.'
